articleText:
[Hacker News — sandromaglione.com]
AI made creating games faster and easier. Yet, making a good game is still hard. This is my answer to the question "If AI implements everything, what's left for me?". Turns out, quite a lot, still.

My "game editor" was a chat, a link to playtest the game, and a web page with previews of 3D models. My "work" was sending text and screenshots. Nothing else.

And still, making those games has been hard and intense. Like never before. For weeks.

AI made writing a game faster and easier. It did not make it easy.

I really enjoy game development. Like, a lot. But game dev is intense, time-consuming, and often has a bad financial return. So much so that I wrote a full essay about my frustration.

A project that used to take months is now a weekend of prompting, and I wanted to see if that holds for a complete game, not just a slop demo.

My goal was getting an answer to the question all game devs are asking themselves:

I found the answer : The hard part didn't go away, it moved. Away from implementation, and into the choices only you can make: what game, what style, what is fun, what is broken.

AI frees your time, so you can think about the core of your game. And that's hard, and now it's all you have to do, all the time. No coding break.

Here are all the steps I will take for my next game, everything that I learned, and how you can steal all of it.

The first decision is yours, and it will always be so: "What game do I want to make?"

The answer you choose has the potential to make or break you and your game. Literally.

Any step in your pipeline the AI can't do becomes your full-time job.

So when you pick a genre and a style, you are also picking where your time will go. Agents go fast, so whatever still needs you becomes the bottleneck. Make sure that step is one worth your time: taste, fun, playtest.

My plan for Spirit Call was a game like Genshin Impact (原神), with a new character every few weeks.

I played Genshin (a lot), and I got fascinated by the characters and their unique designs. Since I am also an illustrator (in training), my initial goal was to design and draw my own characters ( zero AI ), and having them come to life in a game.

But working on a full game with 3D models would take away all my time, leaving none for illustration.

The question became: can the agent turn my designs into high-quality characters, without me stepping in? And, spoiler, the answer was no (after two days of attempts).

Simple stylized models worked well. Detailed anime characters failed every time .

I tried every route I could think of: reference sheets, prebuilt models, a full studio-style pipeline, even copying a character from another game. The results were bad, and worse, never repeatable. And all of this before animation.

I could have done the anime characters by hand (maybe). Even with AI support, one decent character would have taken me weeks.

So I changed the style instead of the game: from full anime characters to simple stylized spirits. Not the initial vision, but one I could ship, fast, with AI in every step of the pipeline.

Even the simple spirits would have cost more by hand than the whole game took: about a month for all ten, against three weeks for all of Spirit Call. With the agent, they took about 20 minutes each:

They were also far easier to animate. Each enemy went through the same steps.

I learned my lesson with my second game, Inkline Town: an ink style, assets made by an agent, with a repeatable pipeline from day one.

Agents are not yet good at anything that requires taste: character design, detailed 3D models, animation, story. Any of it adds more work for you, personally.

If you want an agent-first fast loop, your role should only be playtesting and taste . Anything else, and the loop is broken.

You should not need to read the code. The agent can handle it all. But you need layers of verification on top to make the output reliable. It starts with structure.

I use an Entity Component System (ECS) : every object in the game is an entity, a bag of data (components) like position, velocity or health. Each piece of logic (a system) declares which components it reads and writes, and runs on every entity that has them.

Systems never call each other. That's what makes the architecture composable : the agent can add or rewrite one system without touching the rest, and since every system declares what it touches, the checks have something concrete to verify.

Spawn a Projectile below: it has a position and a velocity, so the same Move system that moves the player moves it too. No new code.

Below is the same rule on a real frame of Spirit Call. The spirit, every enemy and every bolt in flight are entities : pick components, and every entity that has all of them lights up. That is how a system finds what to run on.

On top of that structure, you layer automatic checks. Each one takes a set of bugs off your mind:

The checks run between my prompt and my next play
reactions: [Hacker News] AI driven development doesn't allow you fine enough control to really implement anything specific, you're stuck with whatever generalities the model derives from the prompt on top of whatever random changes and bugs it introduces between iterations. One could take care of those things outside of an LLM, but let's be realistic - for the vast majority of people "making the game f

[Hacker News] I am confident that people using AI to come up with unique and creative ideas will raise above all that slop eventually. It's only a matter for them to embrace AI as well, learn to use it as a tool (and not a replacement), and then indie devs will thrive above the slop.

[Hacker News] It's definitely nice that AI can help speed up some chores of the indie development part that use to take so long before. The sad part is that it's used to flood the current indie markets with slop, either with fully automated crap, or with attempts to steal whatever idea becomes viral to make a quick buck destroying a previously good marketplace. It's a shame that some areas of gam

[Hacker News] Create away. But if you try to sell it, I will assume you are a get-rich-quicker, and I'll warn people against your game like I warn people against MLM schemes or 3d printed tat hawked on Etsy.
[Hacker News] Stop playing games. Just like I stopped reading AI generated blogs. Although that won't happen. There will always be some people passionate to create amazing and fun experiences.
[Hacker News] Fun is a dime a dozen. You can have an LLM tell you jokes all day if you want to. Casino games are fun too. You almost certainly want something more than fun.

items.title: "This Anthropic engineer made this insane first person shooter! And it plays on the browser This is legitimately near war zone quality. The writing is on the wall. Game development will be democratized. The AI games will get less and less sloppy."
